paper_description: This paper introduces a new synchronous multiprocessor mode-change protocol (SM-MDO) and its associated schedulability analysis for multimode real-time systems using global EDF. It specifically addresses the challenge of mode-independent tasks and the potential for lateness propagation during mode transitions, which are not adequately handled by existing protocols without periodicity.

formal_description.statement: A mode-change protocol is said to be synchronous if it schedules new-mode tasks only when all the old-mode tasks have completed. Otherwise, it is said to be asynchronous.
formal_description.conclusion: Classification of mode-change protocols based on when new tasks are enabled relative to old task completion.

informal_sketch.intuition: Synchronous protocols wait for all current tasks to finish before starting new ones, while asynchronous ones might start new tasks earlier.
steps: Check if new-mode tasks are enabled only after all old-mode tasks are finished.
If yes, the protocol is synchronous.
If no, the protocol is asynchronous.
key_insights: Defines a fundamental characteristic of mode-change protocols.

formal_description.statement: A mode-change protocol is said to be 'with periodicity' if and only if it is able to deal with mode-independent tasks. Otherwise, it is said to be 'without periodicity'.
formal_description.conclusion: Classification of mode-change protocols based on their ability to handle mode-independent tasks.

informal_sketch.intuition: Protocols 'with periodicity' can manage tasks that run in all modes, while those 'without periodicity' cannot.
steps: Determine if the protocol can handle tasks that are present in all modes (mode-independent tasks).
If it can, the protocol is 'with periodicity'.
If it cannot, the protocol is 'without periodicity'.
key_insights: Highlights the capability of a protocol to manage tasks that persist across modes.

formal_description.statement: At run-time, we say that a job is active at time-instant t if it has been released at or before time t and it is not completed at time t.
formal_description.conclusion: Defines the state of a job at a specific point in time.

informal_sketch.intuition: An active job is one that has arrived but not yet finished its execution.
steps: Check if a job's release time is less than or equal to the current time t.
Check if the job's completion time is greater than the current time t.
If both conditions are true, the job is active at time t.
informal_sketch.pseudocode:
def is_job_active(job, current_time):
    return job.release_time <= current_time and job.completion_time > current_time
key_insights: Crucial for understanding job states and scheduling progress.

formal_description.statement: At run-time, any task tau_i_k of the application can release jobs if and only if tau_i_k is enabled. Symmetrically, a disabled task cannot release jobs. As such, disabling a task tau_i_k prevents future job releases from tau_i_k. Notice that the MI tasks are enabled at system boot and are never disabled afterwards. When all the MS tasks of a mode (say M_i) are enabled and all the MS tasks of all the other modes are disabled, the application is said to be running in mode M_i (since only the tasks of mode M_i can release jobs).
formal_description.conclusion: Defines the concept of task enablement/disablement and its relation to job releases and system modes.

informal_sketch.intuition: Tasks can be turned on or off. Only 'on' tasks can create new work. When only tasks for a specific mode are 'on', the system is in that mode.
steps: A task is 'enabled' if it can release jobs.
A task is 'disabled' if it cannot release jobs.
Disabling a task stops all future job releases from it.
Mode-Independent (MI) tasks are always enabled.
The system is in Mode M_i if all its Mode-Specific (MS) tasks are enabled and all MS tasks of other modes are disabled.
key_insights: Provides a mechanism to control task execution and define system modes.

formal_description.statement: A scheduling algorithm is sustainable if the schedulability of a task set is not jeopardized by decreasing job execution times or by increasing task periods.
formal_description.conclusion: Defines a property of scheduling algorithms related to robustness against parameter changes.

informal_sketch.intuition: A sustainable scheduler remains fair or better if tasks become 'easier' to schedule (shorter execution, longer periods).
steps: Consider a task set that is schedulable by an algorithm.
If we reduce the execution time of any job or increase the period of any task, the task set must remain schedulable.
If this holds true, the algorithm is sustainable.
key_insights: Ensures that improvements in task parameters don't break schedulability.

formal_description.statement: For a given multimode system tau, multiprocessor platform pi and mode-change protocol P, a validity test V(tau, pi, P) is a condition that indicates a priori whether any transition between any pair (M_i, M_j) of modes of tau meets all the transition deadlines D_j_k(M_i), 1 <= k <= n_j.
formal_description.conclusion: Defines a test to ensure that all transition-specific deadlines are met during mode changes.

informal_sketch.intuition: A validity test checks if the mode-change protocol guarantees that every task in the new mode will be enabled by its specific deadline during any transition.
steps: Identify the system (tau), platform (pi), and mode-change protocol (P).
For every possible transition from mode M_i to mode M_j:
Check if every task tau_j_k in M_j is enabled by its transition deadline D_j_k(M_i).
If all transitions satisfy this, the validity test passes.
key_insights: Focuses on the timely enablement of new tasks during mode switches.

formal_description.statement: For a given multimode system tau, multiprocessor platform pi and mode-change protocol P, a schedulability test S(tau, pi, P) is a condition that indicates a priori whether the execution of tau upon pi, assuming that P is used to manage the mode transitions, meets all the deadlines D_i_k and D_mit_k (forall i, k).
formal_description.conclusion: Defines a test to ensure that all task deadlines (both mode-specific and mode-independent) are met under the given mode-change protocol.

informal_sketch.intuition: A schedulability test checks if, with the chosen mode-change protocol, all tasks (including those that run all the time) will always meet their deadlines.
steps: Identify the system (tau), platform (pi), and mode-change protocol (P).
Analyze the system's behavior over time, considering all possible mode transitions managed by P.
Verify that all Mode-Specific (MS) tasks and all Mode-Independent (MI) tasks meet their respective deadlines.
If all deadlines are met, the schedulability test passes.
key_insights: Ensures system-wide deadline adherence, considering the impact of mode changes.

formal_description.statement: lambda_k of tau_k as lambda_k = C_k / D_k

variables.C_k: worst-case execution time of task tau_k

formal_description.conclusion: Defines the density of a task, which is a measure of its execution demand relative to its deadline.

informal_sketch.intuition: Density is how much work a task demands per unit of time, relative to its deadline. Higher density means more demanding.
steps: Get the worst-case execution time (C_k) of task tau_k.
Get the relative deadline (D_k) of task tau_k.
Calculate density as C_k divided by D_k.
informal_sketch.pseudocode:
def calculate_task_density(task):
    return task.C / task.D
key_insights: Density is a key metric in schedulability analysis, especially for EDF.

formal_description.statement: DBF(tau_k, t) = floor((t - D_k) / T_k) + 1 * C_k

variables.DBF_tau_k_t: Demand Bound Function of task tau_k at time t
variables.C_k: worst-case execution time of task tau_k

formal_description.conclusion: Defines the maximum execution demand of a task tau_k within any time interval of length t.

informal_sketch.intuition: The DBF tells you the maximum amount of execution a single task tau_k can require within any time window of duration t, assuming it has to meet its deadlines.
steps: Calculate the number of full periods that can fit within (t - D_k).
Add 1 to account for a potential job released at the beginning of the interval.
Multiply this count by the worst-case execution time C_k.
key_insights: Provides a fundamental bound on the execution demand of a task.

formal_description.statement: FF-DBF(tau_k, t, sigma) = q_k * C_k + { C_k if r_k >= D_k; C_k - (D_k - r_k) * sigma if D_k > r_k >= D_k - C_k * sigma; 0 otherwise } where q_k = floor(t / T_k) and r_k = t mod T_k

variables.FF_DBF_tau_k_t_sigma: Forced-Forward Demand Bound Function of task tau_k at time t with processor speed sigma
variables.C_k: worst-case execution time of task tau_k
variables.q_k: number of full periods in t
variables.r_k: remainder of t divided by T_k

formal_description.conclusion: Defines the maximum execution demand of a task tau_k within any time interval of length t, considering that execution outside the interval can occur at a speed sigma.

informal_sketch.intuition: FF-DBF is like DBF but accounts for work that might have been done 'before' the interval due to processor speed. It's the maximum execution a task can demand within interval t, considering its execution can be 'sped up' or 'slowed down' by sigma.
steps: Calculate q_k = floor(t / T_k) and r_k = t mod T_k.
If r_k >= D_k, the demand is q_k * C_k + C_k.
If D_k > r_k >= D_k - C_k * sigma, the demand is q_k * C_k + C_k - (D_k - r_k) * sigma.
Otherwise, the demand is q_k * C_k.
key_insights: Accounts for the impact of processor speed on execution demand over an interval.

formal_description.statement: lambda_max(tau_i) = max_{tau_i_k in tau_i} {lambda_i_k}

variables.lambda_max_tau_i: maximum density of tasks in mode M_i
variables.tau_i: set of MS tasks for mode M_i

formal_description.conclusion: Defines the maximum density among all Mode-Specific (MS) tasks within a given mode M_i.

informal_sketch.intuition: This is the highest density found among all the tasks that are specific to mode M_i.
steps: For each task tau_i_k in the set tau_i:
Calculate its density lambda_i_k = C_i_k / D_i_k.
Find the maximum value among all calculated densities.
key_insights: Identifies the most demanding MS task within a mode.

formal_description.statement: lambda_sum(tau_i) = sum_{tau_i_k in tau_i} lambda_i_k

variables.lambda_sum_tau_i: sum of densities of tasks in mode M_i
variables.tau_i: set of MS tasks for mode M_i

formal_description.conclusion: Defines the sum of densities of all Mode-Specific (MS) tasks within a given mode M_i.

informal_sketch.intuition: This is the total density contributed by all tasks that are specific to mode M_i.
steps: Initialize a sum to zero.
For each task tau_i_k in the set tau_i:
Calculate its density lambda_i_k = C_i_k / D_i_k.
Add lambda_i_k to the sum.
key_insights: Represents the aggregate demand of MS tasks in a mode.

formal_description.statement: DBF(tau_i, t) = sum_{tau_i_k in tau_i} DBF(tau_i_k, t)

variables.DBF_tau_i_t: Demand Bound Function of task set tau_i at time t
variables.tau_i: set of MS tasks for mode M_i
variables.DBF_tau_i_k_t: Demand Bound Function of task tau_i_k at time t

formal_description.conclusion: Defines the total maximum execution demand of all Mode-Specific (MS) tasks within a given mode M_i over a time interval of length t.

informal_sketch.intuition: This is the combined maximum execution demand of all tasks specific to mode M_i within any time window of duration t.
steps: Initialize a total demand to zero.
For each task tau_i_k in the set tau_i:
Calculate its Demand Bound Function DBF(tau_i_k, t).
Add this value to the total demand.
key_insights: Aggregates the demand of multiple tasks within a set.

formal_description.statement: FF-DBF(tau_i, t, sigma) = sum_{tau_i_k in tau_i} FF-DBF(tau_i_k, t, sigma)

variables.FF_DBF_tau_i_t_sigma: Forced-Forward Demand Bound Function of task set tau_i at time t with processor speed sigma
variables.tau_i: set of MS tasks for mode M_i
variables.FF_DBF_tau_i_k_t_sigma: Forced-Forward Demand Bound Function of task tau_i_k at time t with processor speed sigma

formal_description.conclusion: Defines the total maximum execution demand of all Mode-Specific (MS) tasks within a given mode M_i over a time interval of length t, considering processor speed sigma.

informal_sketch.intuition: This is the combined maximum execution demand of all tasks specific to mode M_i within any time window of duration t, accounting for processor speed.
steps: Initialize a total demand to zero.
For each task tau_i_k in the set tau_i:
Calculate its Forced-Forward Demand Bound Function FF-DBF(tau_i_k, t, sigma).
Add this value to the total demand.
key_insights: Aggregates the speed-adjusted demand of multiple tasks within a set.

formal_description.statement: LOAD(tau_i) = max_{t>0} (DBF(tau_i, t) / t)

variables.DBF_tau_i_t: Demand Bound Function of task set tau_i at time t

formal_description.conclusion: Defines the load of a task set tau_i, which is the maximum ratio of its demand bound function to the time interval length.

informal_sketch.intuition: The LOAD represents the peak utilization of the task set tau_i over any time interval. It's the highest average demand per unit time.
steps: For every possible time interval length t > 0:
Calculate the Demand Bound Function DBF(tau_i, t).
Compute the ratio DBF(tau_i, t) / t.
Find the maximum value of this ratio.
key_insights: Measures the maximum instantaneous utilization of a task set.

formal_description.statement: FF-LOAD(tau_i, sigma) = max_{t>0} (FF-DBF(tau_i, t, sigma) / t)

variables.FF_LOAD_tau_i_sigma: Forced-Forward Load of task set tau_i with processor speed sigma
variables.FF_DBF_tau_i_t_sigma: Forced-Forward Demand Bound Function of task set tau_i at time t with processor speed sigma

formal_description.conclusion: Defines the Forced-Forward Load of a task set tau_i, which is the maximum ratio of its FF-DBF to the time interval length.

informal_sketch.intuition: This is the peak utilization of the task set tau_i, considering the effect of processor speed sigma. It's the highest average demand per unit time, adjusted for speed.
steps: For every possible time interval length t > 0:
Calculate the Forced-Forward Demand Bound Function FF-DBF(tau_i, t, sigma).
Compute the ratio FF-DBF(tau_i, t, sigma) / t.
Find the maximum value of this ratio.
key_insights: Measures the maximum instantaneous utilization of a task set, adjusted for processor speed.

formal_description.statement: After disabling a task tau, it may be the case that former executions of tau have affected the schedule permanently.
formal_description.conclusion: The execution history of a task can have lasting effects on the schedule even after it's disabled.

informal_sketch.intuition: When a task runs, it uses processor time. Even after it stops running, the time it consumed might have delayed other tasks, and this delay might never be fully recovered.
steps: Consider a task tau that is currently executing.
Observe the schedule and the remaining execution times of other tasks.
Disable task tau.
Continue observing the schedule. If other tasks remain 'later' (have more remaining work) than they would have if tau hadn't run, then tau's former executions had a permanent effect.
informal_sketch.pseudocode:

    # Record state of other tasks (e.g., remaining execution time)
    
    # Disable task_to_disable
    disable_task(task_to_disable)
    
    # Simulate further execution
    # Observe state of other tasks again
    
    # Compare states: if other tasks are permanently 'later', the effect is permanent
key_insights: Highlights the non-local and potentially persistent impact of task execution on the system's state.

formal_description.statement: Even if every mode has been separately asserted to be EDF-schedulable, it may be the case that the lateness produced by the successive executions of the modes propagates through the schedule and ultimately leads to a deadline miss.
formal_description.conclusion: The cumulative effect of lateness from previous modes can cause deadline misses in subsequent modes, even if each mode is individually schedulable.

informal_sketch.intuition: If mode A causes some tasks to finish a bit late, and then you switch to mode B, that lateness can carry over and make tasks in mode B miss their deadlines, even if mode B alone would have been fine.
steps: Assume each mode's task set is individually schedulable (e.g., passes a schedulability test).
Consider a sequence of mode transitions.
Observe if the 'lateness' (tasks finishing after their deadlines or having more remaining work than expected) from one mode's execution accumulates.
If this accumulated lateness causes tasks in a later mode to miss their deadlines, then this observation holds.

    # Track lateness of tasks across transitions
    # Check if any task misses its deadline due to accumulated lateness
    pass
key_insights: Emphasizes the need for system-wide analysis beyond individual mode schedulability.

formal_description.statement: Let sigma >= max_{k=1 to x} {lambda_max(tau_k)}. Let t_0 denote the first instant at which a deadline is missed. Let j_1 denote a job that missed its deadline at time t_0, and let t_1 denote the release time of j_1. From the definitions of s and j_1, we know that j_1 has executed for strictly less than (t_0 - t_1) * sigma execution units over the time interval [t_1, t_0). Let us define the sequence of jobs j_i, time-instants t_i, and an index k, according to the pseudo-code given by Figure 5. Let L denote the length of the interval [t_k, t_0), i.e., L = t_0 - t_k, and let W[t_k, t_0) denote the total amount of execution performed by the m processors within [t_k, t_0). Then, W[t_k, t_0) > (m - (m - 1) * sigma) * L.

variables.lambda_max_tau_k: maximum density of task set tau_k

assumptions: System is not EDF-schedulable upon m processors.
formal_description.conclusion: Provides a lower bound on the total work performed in an interval leading up to a deadline miss, related to processor speed and number of processors.

informal_sketch.intuition: If a system is unschedulable and we consider a processor speed 'sigma' high enough, then in any interval leading up to a deadline miss, the total work done by the processors must exceed a certain threshold related to the interval length and processor speed. This threshold is derived from the fact that the job missing the deadline did not receive enough execution.
steps: Assume a deadline miss occurs at time t_0 by job j_1 released at t_1.
This job j_1 received less than (t_0 - t_1) * sigma execution in [t_1, t_0).

Construct a sequence of jobs j_i and release times t_i based on the pseudo-code in Figure 5 (which essentially traces back the execution and release times of jobs that contributed to the deadline miss).

Let W[t_k, t_0) be the total execution performed by all m processors in [t_k, t_0).
The lemma states that W[t_k, t_0) > (m - (m - 1) * sigma) * L.

formal_description.statement: The contribution of any MI task tau_mit in tau_mit to W[t_k, t_0)_mit is bounded from above by FF-DBF(tau_mit, t_0 - t_k, sigma).

variables.W_t_k_t_0_mit: total work executed by MI tasks in [t_k, t_0)
variables.FF_DBF_tau_mit_t_0_minus_t_k_sigma: Forced-Forward Demand Bound Function of MI task set tau_mit over interval [t_k, t_0) with speed sigma

formal_description.conclusion: The actual work done by MI tasks in an interval is bounded by their FF-DBF over that interval.

informal_sketch.intuition: The maximum amount of work that Mode-Independent (MI) tasks can demand within a specific time interval, considering processor speed, is given by their Forced-Forward Demand Bound Function (FF-DBF).
steps: Consider the interval [t_k, t_0) and the set of MI tasks tau_mit.
Let W[t_k, t_0)_mit be the actual execution performed by these tasks in this interval.
The lemma states that W[t_k, t_0)_mit <= FF-DBF(tau_mit, t_0 - t_k, sigma).
This bound is derived by considering the worst-case scenario for job releases and execution within the interval, adjusted for processor speed.
key_insights: Connects actual work done by MI tasks to their theoretical demand bound, adjusted for processor speed.

formal_description.statement: Let sigma >= max_{k=1 to x} {lambda_max(tau_k)}. Let t_k and t_0 be time instants such that t_k < t_0. Let L = t_0 - t_k. Let W[t_k, t_0) be the total amount of execution performed by the m processors within [t_k, t_0). Then, W[t_k, t_0) <= m * L - (m - 1) * sigma * L + sum_{j=1 to z+1} W[t_mc_j-1, t_mc_j)_j + W[t_k, t_0)_mit.

variables.lambda_max_tau_k: maximum density of task set tau_k
variables.W_t_k_t_0: total execution performed by m processors in [t_k, t_0)
variables.z: number of mode changes in [t_k, t_0)
variables.t_mc_j: time of j-th mode change completion
variables.W_t_mc_j_minus_1_t_mc_j_j: work done by MS tasks of mode X_j in interval j
variables.W_t_k_t_0_mit: work done by MI tasks in [t_k, t_0)

formal_description.conclusion: Provides an upper bound on the total work performed by the m processors in an interval, considering processor speed and work done by MS and MI tasks.

informal_sketch.intuition: This lemma provides an upper bound on the total work done by all processors in an interval. It considers the maximum possible work (m*L), subtracts a term related to processor speed and idle time, and adds the work done by specific modes and MI tasks.
steps: Consider an interval [t_k, t_0) of length L.
The maximum possible work done by m processors is m*L.
The term (m - 1) * sigma * L accounts for potential inefficiencies or processor speed effects.
W[t_k, t_0)_j represents the work done by the MS tasks of the specific mode X_j running during the j-th sub-interval.
W[t_k, t_0)_mit represents the work done by MI tasks.
The lemma states that the total work W[t_k, t_0) is bounded by these components.
informal_sketch.pseudocode:
def bound_total_work_upper(m, L, sigma, work_ms_tasks, work_mi_tasks):
    # This is a conceptual representation of the bound.
    # The actual calculation of work_ms_tasks and work_mi_tasks is complex.
    upper_bound = m * L - (m - 1) * sigma * L + sum(work_ms_tasks) + work_mi_tasks
    return upper_bound
key_insights: Establishes an upper limit on processor utilization within an interval, considering various factors.

formal_description.statement: For any mode X_j running over [t_mc_j-1, t_mc_j) of length L_j, W[t_mc_j-1, t_mc_j)_j <= DBF(tau_Xj, L_j).

variables.W_t_mc_j_minus_1_t_mc_j_j: work done by MS tasks of mode X_j in interval j
variables.tau_Xj: set of MS tasks for mode X_j
variables.DBF_tau_Xj_L_j: Demand Bound Function of task set tau_Xj over interval L_j

formal_description.conclusion: The work done by the MS tasks of a specific mode in an interval is bounded by the DBF of that mode's task set over that interval.

informal_sketch.intuition: During the time a specific mode X_j is active, the total execution performed by its mode-specific tasks cannot exceed the maximum demand they could have within that time interval, as defined by their Demand Bound Function (DBF).
steps: Consider an interval [t_mc_j-1, t_mc_j) where only mode X_j is active.
Let L_j be the length of this interval.
Let W[t_mc_j-1, t_mc_j)_j be the actual work done by the MS tasks of mode X_j.
The lemma states that W[t_mc_j-1, t_mc_j)_j <= DBF(tau_Xj, L_j).
This is because DBF provides the worst-case execution demand for the task set.
key_insights: Relates actual work done by MS tasks to their theoretical demand bound.

formal_description.statement: Suppose that a multimode constrained-deadline sporadic task system tau is not EDF-schedulable upon a platform composed of m processors. Then it holds for all sigma >= max_{k=1 to x} {lambda_max(tau_k)} that W[t_k, t_0) > (m - (m - 1) * sigma) * L.

variables.lambda_max_tau_k: maximum density of task set tau_k
variables.W_t_k_t_0: total execution performed by m processors in [t_k, t_0)

assumptions: System tau is not EDF-schedulable on m processors.
formal_description.conclusion: If a system is unschedulable, then for a sufficiently high processor speed sigma, the total work performed in an interval leading up to a deadline miss is bounded from below.

informal_sketch.intuition: This theorem is the core of the schedulability analysis. It states that if a system is unschedulable, there must be a point in time where the total work done by the processors in a preceding interval exceeds a certain threshold. This threshold depends on the number of processors, the interval length, and a processor speed parameter 'sigma'. This is essentially a condition that must hold if a deadline miss occurs.
steps: Assume the system is not EDF-schedulable.
This implies there exists a first deadline miss at time t_0 by some job j_1 released at t_1.
Define a sequence of jobs j_i and release times t_i (as per Figure 5 in the paper).
Let t_k be the earliest relevant release time in this sequence, and L = t_0 - t_k.
Let W[t_k, t_0) be the total execution performed by all m processors in the interval [t_k, t_0).
The theorem states that W[t_k, t_0) > (m - (m - 1) * sigma) * L, for sigma >= max lambda_max(tau_k).

formal_description.statement: A multimode constrained-deadline sporadic task system tau is EDF-schedulable upon m identical processors, provided that for all intervals [t_k, t_0) and for all sigma >= max_{k=1 to x} {lambda_max(tau_k)}, it holds that W[t_k, t_0) <= m * L - (m - 1) * sigma * L + sum_{j=1 to z+1} DBF(tau_{Xj}, L_j) + FF-DBF(tau_mit, L).

variables.lambda_max_tau_k: maximum density of task set tau_k
variables.W_t_k_t_0: total execution performed by m processors in [t_k, t_0)
variables.z: number of mode changes in [t_k, t_0)

formal_description.statement: Schedulability Test 1 above can be seen as a generalization of the GFB test [20] extended in [21] to constrained-deadline tasks. According to this extension, a task set tau is EDF-schedulable on m identical processors, provided lambda_sum(tau) - lambda_max(tau) / m <= 1.

formal_description.statement: max_{k=1 to n_i} {D_i_k} <= min_{j=1 to x, j!=i} { min_{r=1 to n_j} {D_j_r(M_i)} }

variables.n_i: number of MS tasks in mode M_i
variables.D_i_k: relative deadline of MS task tau_i_k in mode M_i
variables.D_j_r(M_i): relative transition deadline of MS task tau_j_r from mode M_i to M_j

formal_description.conclusion: Condition for the validity of the SM-MDO protocol: the maximum relative deadline of any MS task in a mode must be less than or equal to the minimum transition deadline to any other mode.

informal_sketch.intuition: For the SM-MDO protocol to be valid (meaning all transition deadlines are met), the longest deadline among the tasks of the current mode must be shorter than the earliest deadline by which any task of any *other* mode must be enabled during a transition *from* the current mode. This ensures that when new tasks are enabled after D_max(i) time units, they are all enabled before their respective transition deadlines.
steps: Identify the current mode M_i and the destination mode M_j.
Find the maximum relative deadline D_i_k among all MS tasks tau_i_k in mode M_i.
For every other mode M_j (where j != i), find the minimum transition deadline D_j_r(M_i) for all its MS tasks tau_j_r.
The condition requires that max(D_i_k) <= min(min(D_j_r(M_i))) over all j != i.
This must hold for all possible current modes M_i.
key_insights: Ensures that the fixed delay D_max(i) in SM-MDO is sufficient to meet all transition deadlines.
